mean: so closely united they act as one body and mind
lit: one heart, the same body: two or more people sharing a single mind and body

near.diff: 以心伝心 is understanding each other without words; 一心同体 is being bound together so closely that you share one fate and act as one.
一致団結 is a group pulling together for a goal; 一心同体 stresses an inseparable bond, often between just two parties.

mean: concentrating on one task with no distraction at all
lit: one mind, not scattered: the whole mind held on a single thing

story.text: The phrase comes from the Amida Sutra, which teaches that a person who holds the name of Amida Buddha in mind for one to seven days, with a single mind that does not waver, will see Amida and his attendants appear at the hour of death. From that state of undistracted devotion it came to mean any total concentration.

use.how: Mostly adverbial: 一心不乱に〜する (働く, 祈る, 練習する). Describes someone absorbed in one activity at a given moment, as others see them.

near.diff: 無我夢中 is being so carried away that you lose awareness of yourself; 一心不乱 is steady, single-minded focus on one task.
一生懸命 is trying hard in general; 一心不乱 says the attention never strays from the one thing being done.

mean: settling a matter decisively at one stroke

story.text: The Song-dynasty philosopher Zhu Xi used the image for mastering oneself: selfish desire should be cut off at its root with a single stroke of the blade, once and for all, rather than trimmed bit by bit. use.how: Xを一刀両断にする / 一刀両断に切り捨てる: said of a person who settles a question, rejects a proposal or dismisses an argument outright, in one decisive judgment.

mean: good and bad deeds bring matching consequences
lit: cause and effect answer each other: every deed is repaid in kind

story.text: It is a Buddhist teaching: every act is a cause, and it returns to the one who did it as a matching result, good deeds bringing happiness and bad deeds bringing suffering, whether in this life or a later one. In everyday Japanese today it is said mostly when someone's past wrongdoing comes back on them.

use.how: Said as a comment, 因果応報だ / 因果応報というものだ, about a result seen as the fitting return for someone's earlier conduct, usually bad.

near.diff: 自業自得 blames a person for trouble they brought on themselves; 因果応報 states the general law that deeds come back in kind, good or bad.

mean: firmly resolving to take something on

lit: a bad battle and a bitter fight: struggling against heavy odds

use.how: Xに悪戦苦闘する / 悪戦苦闘の末: said, often with humour, of struggling hard with a difficult task, opponent or object (a machine, a report, a jar lid).

near.diff: 四苦八苦 is having great trouble getting something done; 悪戦苦闘 pictures a battle, often Xと悪戦苦闘する, against a hard task or opponent.
孤軍奮闘 stresses fighting alone without help; 悪戦苦闘 stresses how hard the fight is.
